records.title: Show HN: Taskless, turn AGENTS.md and PR comments into runnable checks
records.author: codedrift_
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm Jakob, the solo dev and founder behind Taskless.

I got tired of my AGENTS.md files being ignored or forgotten a half dozen turns into conversations. I also remembered reading someone here on HN saying we weren't using nearly enough syntax trees in our code checks. This is the result.

Taskless gives you powerful syntax tree tools with human verifiable fixtures. The CLI is MIT licensed, so running the CLI, onboarding, rule writing, and running the underlying ast-grep & Vale checks are all local. You can give it a try with:

npx @taskless/cli

and then asking your agent to "onboard with Taskless".

Under the hood, the CLI works with your agent to read your PR review comments, fixup commits, and agent files. It takes things that keep recurring and turns them into the simplest code-level enforcement that can prevent the issue going forward. By choosing code over an LLM for the runtime, there's no model once code is generated. The checks can then be committed to your codebase and enforced. I'm particularly proud of how determinism is mixed into the onboarding flow. Any time the CLI can give the agent information without letting the agent wandering the codebase, the CLI does. It results in a more consistent experience with far fewer errors. Anonymous telemetry can be disabled outright by setting DO_NOT_TRACK=1 or TASKLESS_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 in your environment (it collects CLI version, OS, the repo's org/owner, and a bit about the repository it's running in).

When the agent's done, it creates a report you can share around to show everyone there's a better way to control the output of agentic coding tools. I thought I'd include a few here from some of my favorite repos.

- Effect: https://tskl.es/gh/Effect-TS/effect/20261104/1g4gRoMmoADlysg... I specifically liked Effect because effect-bot is in the PRs fixing bugs and writing docs for the team, and they already use oxlint plugins and a TypeScript language service plugin.

- Sentry: https://tskl.es/gh/getsentry/sentry/20261016/1ZyMPva1BzaHaa5... Sentry's all open source, and David Cramer's tweeted a lot about determinism, especially now that the team is using Junior to ship code via Slack chat.

- n8n: https://tskl.es/gh/n8n-io/n8n/20261026/1C3I3yVjFyfxNFEpl4qFA... n8n has more AI driven code than the other two repos and is a good example of how bad it can get when the determinism isn't in place. Since agents tend to copy what they see from related files, problems propagate quickly.

I'd love to hear what you're doing today to keep agents behaving, or if you do kick the tires, I'd love the honest feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Gitfold – every Git branch as a folder, ready in a second
records.author: pkuki
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

I want to show you a project which I'm using myself to save time on worktrees creation and management. My case is a bit specific because I'm normally working on a really big monorepo, where creation of a worktree takes around a minute and 20+GB of disk space. Previously I was using a pool of worktrees which were managed by my own sessions manager. It worked, but was a bit clunky and sometimes I was running out of the worktrees anyway.

As a fun side-project I decided to create a VFS for serving git branches directly from the git object store, with only one real checkout needed. I started with read only version to speed-up the reviews (I often checkout the PRs code to get LLM support) and that is very easy to do with FUSE, but it would not let me fully replace my old solution. Adding write capabilities was a bit more involved, and writing without full kernel passthrough turned out to be a few times slower. But interestingly for my workflows it does not matter. I was also running some external tests like full Linux kernel build (allmodconfig) and the performance hit vs a native build was around 2.5%. So far so good!

After building the core I realised that having VFS allows me to play with other interesting features. And I implemented a few:

- tree structure of branch dependencies; you can e.g. have branch 'api', on which 'store' and 'ui' depend. When you add or fetch new commits to 'api', whole tree rebases automatically

- read only views showing "merged" state of each node in the tree from the previous point; e.g. you can check how 'api' branch would look like, if both 'store' and 'ui' would be merged as is; currently it has two modes: only committed or all changes

- command for showing conflicts between current worktree and all other open worktrees

- command for showing all worktrees touching given file of interest

- agents getting real time notifications about potential conflicts

What is also important is that it works without an issue with all native git commands. Git sees those workspaces as normal worktrees. So you can e.g. normally rebase every such worktree separately (which is one of the main differences compared to overlayfs). I'm sure some people will think this project is very similar to GitFS, EdenFS, OverlayFS, ArtifactFS, etc... spoiler alert: it is not. Most of those projects are focusing on fetching objects from remote git server lazily. Which I can imagine is very useful if you need a fresh checkout on a new instance (eg. in a CI). But that is not my use case. I have a full local checkout, and need to be able to create and delete on demand a lot of worktrees. That is it :) But I also prepared a full comparison, just in case: https://github.com/pkukielka/gitfold/blob/main/docs/comparis...

I'm happy to answer any questions!

records.title: Show HN: Biohacking in Chess – can coffee make you a better player?
records.author: srdjanb
records.storyText:
In short:

For the past few years, I've been building a biohacking platform called Plants Research Pro (PRP), designed to help people discover research on bioactive materials and put that research to practical use. Recently, I added a new feature to PRP which is turning out to be my favorite so far: The Chess Lab. This is essentially a set of tools and protocols for biohacking in chess, some of which you can try right now via the link -- I recommend a Single-Session Experiment, which is a 6-test protocol that lets you explore how some intervention, like coffee, might improve your cognitive function in the context of chess.

-

In detail:

The idea for Chess Lab started about four years ago when I came across research by Prof. David O. Kennedy's group showing that sage, cocoa, and other materials can enhance some cognitive functions. If I remember correctly, the subjects were healthy young adults (possibly uni students). I really wanted to test this on myself, and since I like chess, I chose chess as my 'test platform'. I'm not gonna go into the formulation, but I tried sage alone, sage with cocoa, and sage with cocoa and milk. The third mix seemed to give me the best focus and attention (for about 4-6 h), and my rating started to climb after a few weeks. But there was an issue - I had no idea if I was simply improving naturally, or if the mixture was enhancing it. This annoyed me a little bit, and made me realize that PRP needed an N-of-1 experimentation system.

After finally getting around to it, PRP's Experiments system was implemented earlier this year, while Chess Lab was added about a month ago. Both are now live, although testing and refinement are ongoing. The system also supports N>1 experiments, so can be used with a group of people as well.

There are six cognitive tests and a Single-Session Experiment (SSE) to play with for free. The tests are based on those used in cognitive research, while SSE is a simple before-and-after experiment. i.e., you choose an intervention (coffee, tea, exercise, etc.), complete 6 baseline cognitive tests, apply the intervention (drink your coffee or whatever), then repeat the tests to see what changed -- all within a day (or about 1 h for simple SSEs). The results are exploratory, of course, but I think it's pretty cool that I can now do this myself, at home, without going to a university lab.

But I want to make it much better. The signal-to-noise ratio is difficult to estimate, and there are several sources of error. For instance, a chessboard recall test uses positions from real games, but some pawn structures are much easier to memorize than others. I'm examining two approaches: (1) filtering games by board complexity, and (2) introducing random configurations. The thing with (2), though, is that it's less fun and measures a somewhat different aspect of cognition, but that's a story for another day.

For longer experiments, I've added Chess.com statistics, including move accuracy, rating, opponent-adjusted score, etc. And if you're not sure how to set it up, you can describe what you want in plain language (e.g., 'I want to test if lemon peel can improve my chess') and an AI-powered builder will create a research-backed recipe, design the experiment, assign metrics, and select suitable cognitive tests. AI can also help interpret the statistical results. These full experiments are part of the Premium subscription.

In the coming months, I'll add more cognitive tests, analytics, and some ML capability. Most importantly, I hope to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. A new Multi-Session Crossover design (repeated SSEs alternating intervention/no-intervention days, with longitudinal analysis) should help, but there'll definitely be more work needed from different angles.

Anyway, if you like chess and the idea of (safely) optimizing cognitive performance with biohacking, give Chess Lab a try! I'd be very keen for feedback, bug reports, or feature suggestions. Thanks!

records.title: Show HN: Blobby – warns when two coding agents edit the same file (macOS)
records.author: jakobildstad
records.storyText:
Hi HN. I usually run 3-4 coding agents at the same time (Claude Code and Codex), and I kept finding one that had been waiting on a question for 20 minutes without me noticing (bunch of lost time). So I made Blobby. It shows each agent as a blob next to the MacBook notch, so you can see if it's working, done or waiting for you. Click one and you go straight to its terminal tab.

I know there are a lot of notch apps for agents now. What I haven't seen in the others: it warns you when two agents edit the same file, it can give each agent its own git worktree, and when an agent is done it shows what it changed and if the tests passed.

It uses the hooks Claude Code, Codex and Gemini CLI already have, which write the state of each session to a folder on your Mac. No telemetry, and nothing about your sessions leaves your Mac.

Free to try with no signup. Pro is $19 for life. made for macOS 26 on Apple silicon.

I have many plans on improving, but I want to get an inital feel for the response of the concept.

Not related to useblobby.com, which also did a Show HN this month.

records.title: Show HN: Lanlan Jam – a multiplayer DJ booth in the browser
records.author: wchest
records.storyText:
Lanlan Jam is a multiplayer DJ simulator we built for a creators' conference last month: https://jam.lanlan.site

You can put it up on a big screen, then everyone scans a QR code and queues up to take turns “coming on stage” to perform from their phones. It works at an event or your house with friends. There's also a studio mode where you can make loops and tracks on your own and save or share them.

Full disclosure: I am not a DJ and never have been, but I think what people can do with a pair of turntables is fascinating, so went deep into the world of turntables to try to re-create the experience.

This was also a test of what we can build with the primitives of Lanlan.site, the no-code website builder I cofounded. We started it partly to get back to the more creative, fun days of the Internet, when it was easy to make passion sites and share them. Sites on Lanlan are plain html, css, and js. LLMs are good at these, and we didn't want anyone tied to a proprietary framework if they ever wanted to export and move somewhere else.

When I first started building Lanlan Jam, the goal was to push a feature we call live data, simple data channels that let webhook or arbitrary data flow into a page, using the most basic infrastructure possible (which was long-polling…). As we got closer to putting it in front of a wider audience, it turned out, unsurprisingly, that we needed real websockets. So we have just built and added it (still in beta with limited access).

There's a lot more I'd love to do with this, but I wanted to see if it resonates first. Some ideas for what could come next:

- Bring your own music. Let people upload their own tracks, making sure they have the rights to do so.

- A Guitar Hero-style guide that walks you through putting down a track that actually sounds good, with highlights and touch points along the way.

- Remixing. If anyone wants to remix this site and make it better, I'm happy to make you a copy and give you access so you can keep playing with it and improving it. In the future, we’ve been toying with the idea of Git style forking (or remixing) that users could opt in to for specific sites if they wanted other people to be able to take those sites further and remix them and potentially merge them back in after improvements have been made. We are considering adding a Git back end, which would make that easier to manage.

Curious what you think. All feedback welcome!

(Edited for formatting)

records.title: Show HN: Lexis World – a word game for kids who don't need to know any words yet
records.author: piwakawaka
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

In 2018 I released a kids’ app called Lexi’s World. It took me four years to make, and I was very proud of it.

Lexi is a little girl who lives alone on a tiny planet. Kids use a keyboard to type the names of animals and plants, which then join her on the planet. The keyboard only lets you type real words that exist in the game, so it’s made for kids who are just starting to get interested in letters and words.

You can type in DOG and a DOG appears, type in BONE and it has something to eat. Type POND, OTTER, REEDS, DRAGONFLY, FROG, FLY, LILY and add another OTTER and you have a nice little pond scene Type GORILLA three times and you get a family to hang out with There is a lot to discover.

It got some critical acclaim and won three awards, including one I’m especially proud of from a group of US librarians. But it never found a foothold, and it never had any commercial success.

Three weeks ago I had Fable 5.2 convert it to JavaScript, and it solved a problem that had plagued me from day one. Because the game takes place on a planet, gravity shouldn’t pull things to the bottom of the screen. It should pull toward the center of the world, so animals stick to the surface. In Unity I ended up using a plugin that used [shader technique] to render a flat, rectangular world as a sphere. I also spent months trying to build a custom gravity system. It drove me to tears, and I had quaternions coming out of my ears.

When I ported it to JavaScript, I just asked Fable to build a custom gravity system that pulls everything toward the center of the world, and it did.

That got me wondering what else I could do. One weakness of the original was that there weren’t enough things to make. The vocabulary was sparse, and kids quickly discovered everything there was. I’ve now added a lot more, and it’s exciting to watch kids discover what must feel like an endless supply of animals, plants, oceans and more. It’s finally becoming what I always knew it could be.

Here’s my problem. I’m fairly sure I’ve made something that’s really fun for kids, but it’s a website, which means it’s played on a screen. In my mind it’s closer to Sesame Street than to Power Rangers, and the parents most likely to appreciate that are probably the ones who don’t want their kids on a phone. That’s fair enough, and I get that this could be a gateway to screen time. Still, plenty of people carefully manage their kids’ screen time, and I think this could be a good use of it.

I have no idea how to promote it, which is why I’m posting here. I’d love for people to play with it and tell me what they think. I suspect some adults will enjoy it too. I think it’s a lot of fun, anyway.

It’s at https://lexisworld.org. It’s free to play for 15 minutes, and then you can buy a week or a month or a forver pass - as one off payments - no nasty subscriptions.

Thanks for any feedback!

P.S. I also had Fable translate the game and used ElevenLabs to voice the new words. I don’t speak most of these languages, so I really don’t know how good the translations are. I’m not claiming the game properly supports them yet. If you speak one of them, please give it a try and let me know how it holds up.

Hey everyone, I'm Steven. I wanted to share a new project we're working on called Wyrd. It's a real-time verification platform for AI systems. records.title: Show HN: I built Maeto, an SRv6 SD-WAN from scratch on Linux that you can break
records.author: saphalpdyl
records.storyText:
Demo: https://maeto.saphal.me/

GitHub (mirror): https://github.com/saphalpdyl/Maeto

Forgejo instance (issues & planning): https://git.saphal.me/saphalpdyl/Maeto

Small writeups about Maeto: https://blogs.saphal.me/tags/maeto/

---

About 5 months ago, I was tracking osvbng, a vBNG built on VPP. It was mentioned by folks on my previous Show HN, and I saw maintainers talk about Segment Routing support for it. Four months ago, I happened to be in a conversation about SD-WANs (Software-Defined WAN), and it got me thinking about Segment Routing again. So, I started Maeto that evening to learn about traffic engineering.

Maeto intends to be a complete SD-WAN platform: covering everything from the customer edge all the way up to the controller. It draws inspiration from Cato Networks and Google's B4. While initially designed to be a small complete lab, it exploded in scope as things got more and more interesting. And honestly, I'm having a blast.

I just finished implementing high availability (HA) and CE dual-homing. Locally, core detection runs at <50ms and CE (Customer Edge) detection runs at ~300ms (deliberate design since CE-PE edge over public internet). Though in the lab, you may see slightly higher numbers due to softirq saturation because of the random traffic being generated in the background.

Mostly written in Go. Frontend is Elixir Phoenix LiveView (live state is easier there), with C for FRR patches and Python for topology generation. The dashboard is laptop-sized; it's not usable on phones yet. While built with production circumstances in mind, it is far from being production-ready, and will remain a hobby project.

I've got classes and finals coming up. So, I'm presenting this early. I hope I'm allowed to post an update on it in 5-6 months when much cooler things are in place :D

---

Recommended simulation steps if YOU JUST WANNA SEE IT WORK:

- Ideally have 2 tabs of Maeto opened.

- In one of the tabs, go to Operations > Simulator. On stories, run the "PeSLC goes down" story.

- Watch the link-down detection, PLR indicators, and ping loss being <800ms.

---

Known limitations:

- It is emulated. Each node shares the same kernel performing multiple veth hops, encrypt/decrypt, encap/decap per-packet. So, the numbers are not representative and underestimate the performance if it were on dedicated hardware. Performance primarily tanks due to ksoftirq saturation.

- No internet breakout. So, it only supports site-site connections.

- TI-LFA is in the controller and is implemented in its most basic form (more in FAQ). - Only egress protection is implemented, and core P-P links are controller-protected, not local (more in FAQ).

A few questions:

- Maeto does color-based steering (SR policies), and polices bandwidth based on its color. Policing is harsh. It would be ideal for the CE to shape that traffic. This means the classification has to run in the CPE (it runs in PE today). It is just DSCP->color today, but in the future, we may want DPI to classify packets which are not marked. In that case, would it be reasonable to have DPI being done on the CPE which, from my understanding, are light low-compute boxes?

- How do operators tune BFD timers on edges that run on public internet transit (CE-PE edge)? I understand that static timers would be bad when propagation delay may vary. One way I can think of is observing a baseline delay and dynamically tuning BFD based on that?

I answer some of the questions readers may have at https://github.com/saphalpdyl/Maeto#faqs . I would appreciate comments, questions, answers, or feedback from people with operational experience or people who are just curious :)

records.title: Show HN: Iskillz – Turn API docs into API-usage skills for your project
records.author: antelocnova
records.storyText:
Hi there :)

I've created this "skill that makes API skills" because of something that usually happens to me: start a new project, add libraries to it, and then agents I use don't know how to make the most of those libraries.

And that's usually because agents don't get much the APIs provided by the libraries, and then start making assumptions, working on a "figuring it out as we go" basis, which usually leads to messy code where intent is lost.

Usually, the documentation for an API is structured very similarly to a documents tree: an index (root), and a hierarchy of documents under it, most often not a very deep one.

Also, for complex skills, we have skill trees, where a root SKILL.md refers a hierarchy of other sub-skills under it, so agents can navigate the tree in order to find the right sub-skill for the task at hand.

Which gave me the following idea: take an API documents tree, its taxonomy too, and then derive a skill tree from those.

Do this for an API's docs set, and you'll get an equivalent skill tree for that API, ready to be navigated by agents, in order to find the right subset of functions, datatypes, etc. to be applied to the case at hand.

This is what iskillz does: it provides the knowledge and tooling for my agent to inspect the API docs for some library I use, produce a skill tree for it, and then add that new skill to the current project, so the same agent can make the best use of the library's API.

Repo: https://github.com/anteloc/iskillz

records.title: Show HN: KradleBench – Multi-agent AI evals in Minecraft
records.author: jamest
records.storyText:
Hi HN -

This is James and Kemal. In past lives we led Firebase and Tensorflow/JAX respectively. HN has been a particularly big part of my (James’) career and the trajectory I’ve taken would be meaningfully different without it. Thank you!

Our team shipped a benchmark: KradleBench. We test AI in Minecraft Worlds.

1. The worlds are multi-agent. Humans and other AIs are in there too, often pursuing their own goals. Collaboration and conflict skills fall out of this property.

2. The world are dynamic. They constantly change, which means that agents need to react. “Capture the Flag” has a single winning condition, and many different ways to achieve it. This leads to many emergent and creative strategies.

3. The worlds are real-time. They are not turn-based, they do not wait for AIs to finish thinking. Nature balanced speed and intelligence in humans, we can understand this in AIs too.

Underneath all this is Kradle, a platform to test and understand intelligence. It’s a petri dish where any intelligence type (LLM, World Model, Human) can be compared and generate useful information to improve current systems, whether it’s on capabilities or safety.

Some findings so far: - A skilled human was #1, until yesterday when Astra 6.2 surpassed them. We lose badly on solo tasks and out-compete on multi-agent ones - Astra 6.2 iterates on its strategy 4x faster than Fable 5.2. The Claude family tends to think hard and stick with strategies. The OpenAI models tend to be more reactive and iterative, which serves them well in multi-agent, dynamic, real-time evals.

We’ve got videos on all the top model’s page, and we’ll be producing them when a new model launches. Sign up on the site to get them and for when the platform opens.

Thanks for reading,

James & Kemal

records.title: Show HN: Mapped wild edible plants and fungi near you
records.author: sriacha
records.storyText:
In a rabbit hole learning about edible plants/fungi over the last few years I often would check inaturalist.org to see if certain species were nearby, and often wished I could just filter out edible species.

Over the past few months I've been working on creating a global database of edible (and to a lesser extent medicinal) species from many disparate sources, and edibilia.org cross references these with inaturalist (and a few other ocurrence data sources).

The map and taxa browser also include fairly powerful filters; ie filter by source (specific books, papers, websites), geographic filtering, morphological filtering, etc.

Lots to do still but I think its at a pretty useful point, happy for any feedback.

records.title: Show HN: Type prompts directly in terminal shell to kickoff Claude and codex
records.author: quan
records.storyText:
I kept entering coding instruction in the shell by mistake, so I built this shell plugin to intercept the command not found error and pass the prompt to coding agent instead. Now I can type in plain English such as "work on the next task in PLAN.md", and it opens claude code in that directory.

It makes sure regular commands such as `git status` still run as usual. When the shell can't find a command, llmao first checks for likely typos before treating it as a prompt. So it'll suggest git if the command is gti status. It works with zsh, bash, and Fish.

records.title: Show HN: TripleClick – 220-line Mac menu bar app for trackpad middle click
records.author: w222
records.storyText:
I was a paid user of BetterTouchTool for years, but I eventually realized I only used it for one thing: three-finger trackpad click = middle click. TripleClick is a small app that does just that, for free.

It never connects to the internet, so there's no telemetry.

It's ~220 lines of Swift. Apple's private MultitouchSupport framework counts the fingers on the trackpad, and a CGEventTap turns a click with three fingers down into a middle click.

It also supports an optional middle-drag: click with three fingers, lift two, and drag with one. This way, it doesn't conflict with the standard 3-finger gestures for Mission Control and App Exposé.

This app is now my daily driver. Check it out & let me know what you think.

MIT licensed, macOS 13+. Not notarized; the README covers installing.
